prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: Seven of eight of us ranked the optical lattice clock, and I think the support reflects substance rather than habit. The magic-wavelength idea is a simple piece of atomic physics: choose the lattice wavelength so the light shift is equal for both clock states, and the atoms can be held for a long time without the trap disturbing the transition. Katori proposed it and demonstrated early strontium lattice clocks, and Ye's group took the system to record accuracy and stability and showed that many atoms interrogated together are a resource, not only a nuisance. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST, NPL) now reproduce 10^-18 performance, and clock-to-clock comparisons, including over fibre links, agree. The same devices resolve the gravitational redshift over millimetre-to-centimetre height differences, and they give new limits on drifting constants and on certain dark-matter models. That is a measurement that shows something about nature, with a clear and fair two-person attribution, which is what I would want from a Nobel Prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to what has already been honoured. The frequency comb (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and ion-trap quantum control, including the ion-clock programme (Wineland, 2012), already covered the neighbouring precision-spectroscopy ground, and a sceptic could say the lattice clock is a refinement, albeit a spectacular one. There is also a metrological timing argument: the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and some colleagues may prefer to wait for it. Finally, the Katori and Ye pairing omits others who made real contributions (Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Derevianko and Pal'chikov on the theory of magic wavelengths and light-shift systematics, and the ion-clock groups at NIST). I think none of these defeats the case, but they are legitimate, and I have not checked the present record uncertainties and the early priority dates beyond my memory.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a textbook case of a measurement technique that pushed precision by orders of magnitude, and he flags that the earlier comb and ion-trap prizes may be seen as having covered part of this territory.
responses.response: I agree on the merit and want to sharpen the answer to the overlap worry. The comb is the gearbox that counts optical cycles and the ion clock uses a single trapped particle; the lattice clock adds a different physical idea, namely cancelling the trap's light shift at the magic wavelength so that a very large ensemble can be interrogated without perturbation. That is what made 10^-18 stability reachable in hours rather than weeks, and it is why the prize can be framed as a new principle and not as a third prize for the same ladder. I part from Stefan slightly on the 'wait for the second's redefinition' point: the science is settled whether or not the CGPM acts, and a prize that waits for a bureaucratic milestone risks rewarding the milestone rather than the discovery.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube first as an instrument-driven opening of a new observational window, and ranks the lattice clock third, noting that the strontium-ion and Al+ clocks are competitors and raising the question of which system defines the prize.
responses.response: I take the IceCube case seriously and defer to Mark and Ulf on the astrophysics; a new window on the universe is exactly the kind of thing that should be rewarded. My reservation is only about the attribution Mark himself raises: a thousand-person collaboration, the AMANDA and Baikal precursors, and source evidence at roughly 4 sigma for NGC 1068, which is good but not yet the kind of settled picture I look for. On his competitor point, I would say the Al+ ion clock is a real rival in accuracy, but it is the lattice clock that reaches the best stability and that is spread across many laboratories, and the prize would not be about the species but about the principle of magic-wavelength trapping and its consequences. The citation I propose is deliberately framed on that principle, so it does not exclude ion clocks as a separate achievement already recognised in 2012.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first and the twisted-bilayer-graphene trio second, and puts the lattice clock third, praising it as clear and original with large impact and seeing a two-laureate configuration as clean.
responses.response: We agree that the clock is clean and mature, and I appreciate that Ulf names the attribution as fair. Where I would qualify his ranking is on twisted bilayer graphene: the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is a beautiful story, but several of us (Olle, Bernhard and Olsson) note that the superconducting pairing mechanism is unresolved, and Olle even calls it slightly early. I am not competent to judge the condensed-matter details, so I defer to the condensed matter colleagues, yet I notice that this is precisely the maturity criterion on which the clock is strongest. If the committee wants a two-part prize, I would rather pair the clock with a discovery whose interpretation is settled than with one that still has its central mechanism in debate.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics first for their exact, model-independent character, while acknowledging that priority among Evans, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert is contested and that he ranks the lattice clock only fifth, asking whether it is a physics-prize-significant step after previous clock and comb prizes.
responses.response: I find Bernhard's emphasis on exact and general results attractive, and the experimental verification in RNA pulling and colloids is real. But the three-person limit forces a hard cut among Evans, Jarzynski, Crooks, Cohen, Morriss, Searles and Seifert, and Bernhard says so himself; that attribution problem is far worse than for the clock, where the two names track the two decisive steps. On his significance question, I would answer that a lattice clock redefines what we can measure and has already produced a laboratory test of the gravitational redshift over a millimetre scale, so it carries both a conceptual and a practical consequence. I would be willing to hear a case that fluctuation theorems deserve a place in a two-part prize, but I would need to see a defensible three-name set first.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second.
Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names, or whether Lemonde, Derevianko or the ion-clock groups should shape the citation; I rely on memory for the early lattice-clock priority.

If a two-part prize is wanted, which second achievement (cold-atom quantum simulation, atom interferometry, or a condensed-matter or astroparticle topic) has the most settled interpretation and a clean three-name credit.
Whether the committee views atom interferometry (B043) as one discovery or a technique, and whether the Chu overlap can be handled.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for the preferred B007 (Katori and Ye); I have no documented collaboration with either. For the record, I have collaborated closely with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and with Ursula Keller's group at ETH, so I would need to weigh recusal on B003 (Ti:sapphire and mode-locking, which credits Keller), and I note that Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato, not shortlisted, are my collaborators. I also flag that atom-interferometry and cold-atom candidates (B043, B041) are in my own broad AMO field, where I know the literature well but have no personal link to the credited names.
